4.text: Some of the Asiatic Eskimo also bring sacrifices to Kereˊtkun and to

5.text: his wife. By them, Kereˊtkun is called Kaˊcak. Allowing for the necessary

6.text: phonetical changes, it is probably the same name.

7.text: It is hard to tell with which tribe this idea of the sea Deity originated.

8.text: The Eskimo at Indian Point assert that the Chukchee sacrifices to Kereˊtkun

9.text: are more complicated, though I am not sure that such is really the case.

10.text: Furthermore, most of the religious ideas of the Maritime Chukchee are

11.text: related to those of the Reindeer branch, while Kereˊtkun and his ritual stand

12.text: quite apart. The Reindeer people do not consider Kereˊtkun a Chukchee

13.text: Deity proper, and assert that he is a sea-god, and that he belongs to the

14.text: Maritime people, particularly to the Eskimo. The Eskimo of Indian Point

15.text: sacrifice also to the old woman living at the bottom of the sea. She is

16.text: called Nuliˊṛahak (“big woman”). She has also another name, which it is

17.text: considered sinful to pronounce outside of the ceremonials, and which I could

18.text: not ascertain by any means I could devise.

19.text: “House-beings” (yaˊra-vaˊɪrg̣ɪt) are the “spirits” of tents or of houses, and

20.text: exist more or less independent of the family living in the house. They outlive

21.text: generations of inmates of the house; but, if the house itself is destroyed,

22.text: they perish with it. If the tent is forsaken by the inhabitants, and left in

23.text: the open, as sometimes happens with the Reindeer Chukchee, the “house-

24.text: spirits” turn into very dangerous “earth-spirits.” According to the Chukchee,

25.text: this is because everything that has been connected with man, and has broken

26.text: away from this relation, becomes spoiled and wicked.

27.text: “House-spirits” have names that are derived from stems which mean

28.text: “absence of motion.” They usually live in pairs, as husband and wife, and

29.text: have children, who are liable to disease and are mortal. For instance, a

30.text: shaman of the country of Anadyr told me that the “spirit” of his house had

31.text: the name Olvaˊɪrg̣ɪn (“motionless”), and his wife was called Vêˊtča-ñeˊut

32.text: (“standing-woman”).¹ Both of these were young. Three years ago they had

33.text: a son, whom the shaman himself unintentionally killed in the following

34.text: manner. One night, hearing the sound of walking in the outer tent, and

35.text: believing it to come from “keˊlet,” he threw out of the sleeping-room some

36.text: urine from the chamber-vessel as an effective means of driving them off. Then

37.text: he heard the low groan of a child, and knew that something was wrong

38.text: with his own “house-spirits.” In the morning his little child, who had been

39.text: slightly ailing for a few days, suddenly died. Both he and his “house-spirit”

40.text: thus became childless. The “house-spirit,” in order to replace his loss, had
